RAG and Gemma: A Winning Combination for Incorporating Generative AI into Your Business.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that enhances the responses of Large Language Models (LLM) by allowing the incorporation of additional knowledge provided by the user. This way, the models can generate content tailored to specific use cases.
In this tutorial, we will provide the LLM model (Gemma) with a set of documents containing specific information on the topics that interest us, so that it uses exclusively that knowledge to answer user questions.
We will use models from Google’s Open Models family: Gemma, specifically version 2 with 2 billion parameters: gemma2_instruct_2b_en. To facilitate implementation, we will also use LangChain. We will create a notebook in Google Colab, so you must first accept the terms and conditions of use for Gemma and generate your Kaggle credentials.
Basically, the steps to implement RAG are:
1.
Indexing: Create the Vector Database with specific documents on the topics that interest us.
2.
Retrieval: Configure the LLM model to generate responses using primarily information from the Vector DB.
3.
Execution: Ask questions and validate that the responses are obtained mainly from the provided documents.
Let’s get started :)
Step 1. Create the Vector Database with specific documents on the topics that interest us. (INDEXING)
In this step, we must add the documents we want the model to use to answer questions to a Vector Database. For this example, we will use a PDF about the Sustainable Development Goals.
We will have 2 folders:
•
My Data: Will store the documents in PDF format with the information of interest. You can add one or multiple documents.
•
VectorDB: Will contain the vector database in Chroma DB.
The PDFs located in the “My Data” folder will be divided into chunks and each chunk will be converted into a numerical representation (embedding) using pretrained models.
Embeddings provide a numerical vector representation of the text, allowing comparison and finding similarities between different chunks. This way, by comparing these numerical representations, we can identify relevant chunks in response to the user’s questions.
The code to read the files and process them is as follows:
# Reading the PDFs from the configured directory loader = PyPDFDirectoryLoader(source_data_folder) data_on_pdf = loader.load() # number of pages loaded print(len(data_on_pdf)) # Partitioning the data. With a delimited size (chunks) and 200 characters of overlapping to preserve context text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter( separators=[" ", " ", ". ", " ", ""], chunk_size=1000, chunk_overlap=200 ) splits = text_splitter.split_documents(data_on_pdf) # Number of chunks obtained print(len(splits)) #We will use Hugging Face embeddings # https://huggingface.co/sentence-transformers/all-MiniLM-L6-v2 embeddings_model = SentenceTransformerEmbeddings(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
Now we will store the embeddings in the vector database: Chroma DB. For this, we will use LangChain utilities.
# Store the chunks in the database vectorstore = Chroma.from_documents(documents=splits, embedding=embeddings_model, persist_directory=path_db)
2. Configure the LLM model to generate responses based primarily on the information retrieved from the vector database (Retrieval).
We will start by downloading Gemma 2 to our Google Colab notebook
from langchain_google_vertexai import GemmaChatLocalKaggle keras_backend: str = "jax" model_name = "gemma2_instruct_2b_en" llm = GemmaChatLocalKaggle( model_name=model_name, model=model_name, keras_backend=keras_backend, )
We will implement a results parser to extract the relevant part of the response generated by Gemma.
# Helpers from langchain_core.output_parsers import BaseTransformOutputParser class GemmaOutputParser(BaseTransformOutputParser[str]): """OutputParser that parses LLM response and extract the generated part.""" @classmethod def is_lc_serializable(cls) -> bool: """Return whether this class is serializable.""" return True @property def _type(self) -> str: """Return the output parser type for serialization.""" return "gemma_2_parser" def parse(self, text: str) -> str: """Return the input text with no changes.""" model_start_token = "model " idx = text.rfind(model_start_token) return text[idx + len(model_start_token) :] if idx > -1 else "" def format_docs(docs): return " ".join(doc.page_content for doc in docs)
We will use the Chroma DB database as the information source for the retriever and define a prompt that guides the model to generate responses based on the provided context.
retriever = vectorstore.as_retriever() # https://smith.langchain.com/hub/rlm/rag-prompt?organizationId=6467f92b-9dac-5816-964f-8abcfa4e4456 prompt = hub.pull("rlm/rag-prompt")
Prompt: You are an assistant for question-answering tasks. Use the following pieces of retrieved context to answer the question. If you don’t know the answer, just say that you don’t know. Use three sentences maximum and keep the answer concise. Question: {question} Context: {context} Answer:
Finally, we will create a RAG chain that integrates all the components and allows us to get responses from the model based on the relevant information from our documents.
rag_chain = ( # Retrieve documents relevant to the question {"context": retriever | format_docs, "question": RunnablePassthrough()} # The result will fill the `{question}` # and `{context}` variables of the prompt | prompt # The complete prompt will be sent to the LLM | llm # The model's response will be parsed by GemmaOutputParser | GemmaOutputParser() )
3. Ask questions and validate the responses (Execution).
Remember that the document we used contains information on the Sustainable Development Goals, so we can start asking questions about it.
The code we used to send questions to the model is quite simple:
# @title Questions to the Document pregunta = "What goals are related to education?" # @param {type:"string"} response = rag_chain.invoke(pregunta ) Markdown(response)
All these responses are generated using an “Open Model”, so there are no costs incurred for text size (tokens) or frequency of use. This makes it an ideal option for generative artificial intelligence initiatives in your business or startup.
